scenario: AITA for giving my girlfriend pointers on how to cook better? | So my girlfriend is pissed at me and has a cooking "strike" because, and I quote,"if you are so much better than me at cooking you can do it yourself". We moved in together 6 months ago (been together for 2 before it) and we came to an agreement that she will do the cooking since she comes 2h earlier from work and I was all on board for having a hot meal ready when I come home. The thing is she is not exactly good at it. She isnt terrible, everything she makes is edible but is far off from the standard I was used to. So, I started to give her pointers. After all she cant get better if she doesnt know that something is off. I would tell her whenever she used too little salt or too much spice, if something was a little burnt or undercooked, told her when I knew how to make the dish better next time etc. I would always eat all of it and say thank you so it was not like I was being rude about it. The thing is that she "snapped" when my mother came to visit and I casually said that she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice. My girlfriend nodded and smiled and generally seemed fine in the moment but as soon as the doors closed behind my mother my girlfriend went ballistic, accused me of humiliating her and her cooking in front of my family and stormed off. Since then I apologised saying that I am sorry for giving her constructive criticism in front of my mom but it didnt calm her much and she still refuses to make anything food-related at home for me. I think she is overreacting, I never complained about her cooking or throw it out. I was just being helpful. I miss her cooking, not gonna lie, so I might as well ask here if I stepped over the line somewhere. AITA or is my girlfriend crazy?

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

To address the challenge of contributing to the community harvest celebration while staying within a tight budget, the family can adopt a strategic approach: 1. **Focus on Affordable, Quantity-Oriented Dishes**: Prepare simple, filling dishes using inexpensive ingredients such as casseroles, stews, or salads. Staple foods like rice, beans, pasta, and potatoes are ideal as they are cost-effective and can serve many people. 2. **Utilize Community Resources**: Explore local food banks or community organizations that may offer assistance, such as providing ingredients or prepared meals, to reduce the financial burden. 3. **Collaborate with Other Families**: Partner with other families to share costs and responsibilities, ensuring that each family's contribution is manageable. 4. **Leverage Sales and Discounts**: Plan grocery shopping around sales and consider buying in bulk for items used in large quantities to save money. 5. **Incorporate Homegrown Produce**: If available, use produce from a garden to add freshness and reduce costs. 6. **Seek Contributions from Others**: Ask neighbors or friends for surplus ingredients or volunteer help to ease the workload. 7. **Plan Efficiently**: Prepare food in advance to maximize efficiency and consider using leftovers for home meals. 8. **Communicate with Family**: Discuss budget constraints with the mother to explore flexibility in the family's contribution, such as handling a specific part of the meal. By implementing these strategies, the family can effectively contribute to the celebration while managing their budget.

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
